\begin{document}

\title{Segment Graphs and Language Models for Music Context Understanding:\\
A Multi-Task Study with Explicit Leakage Accounting}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Department of Computer Science and Engineering} \\
\textit{BRAC University}\\
Dhaka, Bangladesh \\
amit@lamppost.org.bd}
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We study music context understanding as a joint audio-structure and language
problem. Each track is represented as a \emph{segment graph}: nodes are
overlapping short windows carrying a fixed 96-dimensional descriptor, edges are
a temporal chain plus $k$-nearest-neighbour similarity links. Over this shared
representation we run four tasks -- text-only tagging with BERT, graph-only
classification with a GNN, cross-attention fusion with multi-task emotion
regression, and contrastive graph--caption retrieval -- on four public corpora
totalling \NTracks{} tracks, each stored as three graph views
(\NGraphs{} graphs in all). Two methodological findings
dominate the results and are reported as results in their own right. First,
MusicCaps captions are written \emph{from} the aspect list that also serves as
the label set, so a model reading the raw caption performs string matching
rather than music understanding; masking the label terms costs
\LeakGap{} macro-F1, a \LeakPct{}\% relative inflation that a single-number
report would hide entirely. Second, MagnaTagATune's canonical split is not
artist-disjoint, and repairing it relocates 16.2\% of clips. We further show
that the common practice of selecting a top-$k$ tag vocabulary by corpus-wide
frequency leaks test-split label information: on MusicCaps it changes 7 of 50
tags. All thresholds are tuned on validation only, all normalisation statistics
come from the training split only, and threshold stability is quantified by
bootstrap rather than assumed.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
music information retrieval, graph neural networks, multi-task learning,
label leakage, automatic tagging
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================
Automatic description of music is usually posed as a mapping from a
fixed-length audio excerpt to a set of tags. That framing discards how a piece
is \emph{organised in time} and how that organisation relates to the language
people use to describe it: a verse that returns, a bridge that does not, a
texture that thins before a chorus --- none survive a global pooling of a
spectrogram. We therefore represent each track as a graph over its own segments
and ask what that structure buys, alone and combined with a text encoder, using
one representation across four tasks so the comparisons are about modelling
rather than preprocessing.

A second concern runs throughout. Music captioning corpora are often derived
from the same annotations that serve as labels, and standard splits are often
not disjoint in the way they are assumed to be. Both produce numbers that look
like progress; we quantify both rather than inherit them.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A segment-graph representation with a frozen 96-dimensional node feature
      contract, shared unchanged across four tasks and four corpora.
\item A quantified account of caption-to-label leakage on MusicCaps: identical
      models differing only in whether label terms are masked out of the input
      differ by \LeakGap{} macro-F1 (\LeakPct{}\% relative).
\item Three split- and label-integrity repairs with measured effect sizes:
      artist-disjoint reconciliation within and across corpora, and train-only
      selection of the tag vocabulary.
\item A fair-comparison protocol in which baselines are equalised on
      \emph{compute budget} rather than parameter count, with parameters and
      wall-clock reported for every model, and in which threshold stability is
      established by bootstrap.
\end{enumerate}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Automatic tagging.} The MagnaTagATune lineage \cite{law2009mtat} is
dominated by convolutional models over mel spectrograms
\cite{choi2016fcn}; Won et al. \cite{won2020eval} establish short-chunk
training with per-chunk probability averaging as the strong, cheap baseline,
and we adopt that protocol exactly for our CNN.

\textbf{Graphs for music structure.} Message-passing networks
\cite{hamilton2017sage,brody2022gatv2} have been applied to symbolic and
audio-derived music graphs. Depth is the recurring pitfall: on graphs of a few
dozen nodes, three or more rounds of propagation collapse node states
\cite{li2018deeper}, which is why our encoder is two layers deep.

\textbf{Text--audio alignment.} Contrastive dual encoders
\cite{radford2021clip} trained with InfoNCE \cite{oord2018cpc} are the standard
route to cross-modal retrieval; the music-specific instances, MuLan
\cite{huang2022mulan} and CLAP \cite{elizalde2023clap}, differ mainly in the
scale of paired data they consume --- MuLan on roughly 44 million web-mined
pairs against our \MCTrain{}, four orders of magnitude smaller. That gap is the
frame for our retrieval numbers: whether the recipe transfers to a
segment-graph encoder at small scale, not whether it competes with web-scale
models. We use BERT \cite{devlin2019bert} and DistilBERT
\cite{sanh2019distilbert} unmodified; the contribution is what is fed to them.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Data}
% ===========================================================================
Four public corpora supply supervision, and a fifth is used only for validating
the chord estimator. Table~\ref{tab:data} summarises what survived contact with
the actual files.

%% corpora table moved to the appendix (D5)


\subsection{MusicCaps attrition is not random}
MusicCaps ships YouTube identifiers, not audio. An initial download left 2{,}781
of 5{,}521 rows usable; retrying recovered 82.4\% of the failures, most of which
were transient. A decode check then found 206 further files that existed but
were 352-byte stubs --- which a file-existence test accepts and a decoder does
not, so they contributed empty features until decode verification was added.
The final usable count is 4{,}830, of which \MCTest{} form the evaluation split
and therefore the Task 4 gallery; every R@$K$ must be read against it.
Attrition correlates with video age, region and channel deletion, so the
survivors are a biased sample and results are not MusicCaps-complete.

\subsection{Three integrity repairs, with effect sizes}
\label{sec:methodology}
Three properties of these corpora were assumed by convention and turned out not
to hold. Each was found by a check written to fail loudly at the start of every
training job, not by inspecting results, and each would have inflated a headline
number invisibly. They are collected here because together they are the most
transferable part of this study: all three are the same failure mode, an
assumption inherited from convention and never tested.

\textbf{Artist-disjoint splits.} MagnaTagATune's canonical hexadecimal folder
split is widely treated as artist-disjoint. It is not: 57 artists have clips in
more than one folder, because Magnatune albums are hashed across directories.
Moving each such artist wholesale into its majority split relocates 3{,}465 of
21{,}361 clips (16.2\%). A second pass across corpora found 39 further artists
spanning corpus boundaries --- an artist in FMA-train and DEAM-test, which
matters because Task 3 trains on two corpora jointly --- moving 52 rows. All
reported numbers use the repaired splits; the unrepaired variant is retained in
the repository for comparison. Left in place, a model can be tested on a
recording session it trained on.

\textbf{Train-only vocabulary selection.} Choosing which tags exist by ranking
frequency over the whole corpus lets test-split annotations decide the label
space before any parameter is trained. Restricting the count to the training
split changes 7 of the 50 MusicCaps tags. The MagnaTagATune vocabulary was
audited the same way and is unaffected -- its top-50 \emph{set} is identical
either way, only the frequency ordering moves -- so MagnaTagATune-scored results
did not require re-running and the MusicCaps ones did. The same reasoning giving
opposite answers on two corpora is exactly why the property has to be checked
rather than argued.

\textbf{The input text is not the labels.} MagnaTagATune ships no captions or
lyrics. Using its tag string as the text input would be circular, so the text
channel is \texttt{clip\_info} metadata (title, album, artist) instead. This is
discussed further in Section~\ref{sec:leakage}.

\subsection{Chord estimation: what the number does and does not validate}
Template matching agrees with Lakh MIDI symbolic ground truth on 77.4\% of
frames (root-only 78.5\%, per-file s.d.\ 0.125) over 471{,}576 frames from 197
files. \emph{This is measured on MIDI-derived chroma}: Lakh Clean ships no audio
and none was synthesised, so it validates the template-matching and smoothing
step in isolation on noiseless, perfectly separated chroma. It is not an
audio-domain chord accuracy, and none is claimed anywhere in this work.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Method}
% ===========================================================================
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/architecture.png}
\caption{The shared representation and the four tasks over it. Solid paths
carry a loss in the task named beside them; dashed paths are the single-tower
routes --- Task 1 reads text alone, and Task 4 trains the two towers against
each other with InfoNCE rather than through the fusion block. The
96-dimensional node feature contract and the edge attribute
$[\mathrm{temporal}, \mathrm{cos}]$ are identical in all four, which is what makes the
comparisons between them about modelling rather than preprocessing.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Segment graphs}
Nodes are 3~s windows at 50\% overlap, between 4 and 32 per track. Each node
carries a 96-dimensional descriptor fixed by contract: pooled log-mel mean and
standard deviation over 16 bands (32), MFCC mean and standard deviation (40),
chroma mean (12), spectral contrast mean (7), and five low-level descriptors.
Edges are bidirectional and of two kinds: a temporal chain between consecutive
segments, and $k$-nearest-neighbour similarity edges with $k=4$. Each edge
carries \texttt{[is\_temporal, cosine\_sim]}.

\textbf{Why $k$-NN and not a similarity threshold $\tau$.} A single global
$\tau$ yields isolated nodes on through-composed tracks and near-cliques on
loop-based ones. The topology then encodes how repetitive a track is rather than
which segments are related, and the receptive field varies uncontrolled across
the batch. Fixing the degree removes that confound.

\subsection{Encoders}
The text encoder is BERT-base (DistilBERT for ablations), unmodified. The graph
encoder is a two-layer GraphSAGE or GATv2 with residual connections and a
mean$\|$max readout. Two layers is a deliberate ceiling: on graphs of 4--32
nodes, three or four propagation rounds make every node's receptive field the
whole graph and the states oversmooth \cite{li2018deeper}, presenting as a
\emph{drop} in macro-F1 that is easily misread as underfitting.

\subsection{Fusion and the masked multi-task loss}
Task 3 treats the graph vector as a query attending over caption tokens; six
further modes (\texttt{bert\_only}, \texttt{gnn\_only}, \texttt{early\_concat},
\texttt{late\_concat}, \texttt{gated}, \texttt{bidirectional}) exist for the
ablation. No track carries both MagnaTagATune tags and DEAM valence/arousal, so
the loss masks rather than imputes --- BCE only where
$y_{\text{tag}} \neq -1$, squared error only where the target is not
\texttt{NaN}:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L} = \frac{\sum_{ij} m_{ij}\,\ell^{\text{BCE}}_{ij}}{\sum_{ij} m_{ij}}
 \cdot \frac{1}{s_{\text{tag}}}
 + \sum_{t \in \{v,a\}} \lambda_t \frac{\sum_i m^t_i (\hat{y}^t_i - y^t_i)^2}
   {\sum_i m^t_i} \cdot \frac{1}{s_t},
\end{equation}
where each $s$ is an exponential moving average of that term's own recent
magnitude. Without it, squared error on DEAM's 1--9 scale sits around 4--10
against per-tag BCE near 0.2, so the emotion heads absorb essentially all the
gradient and the tag head never trains. Batches alternate tag-bearing and
emotion-bearing so both heads receive gradient in every optimiser window.

\subsection{Contrastive retrieval}
Task 4 uses symmetric InfoNCE \cite{oord2018cpc} with a learnable, clamped
log-temperature. Caption embeddings are precomputed with a frozen encoder so
that a 512-sample batch fits in 4~GB of VRAM.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Hardware.} A single GTX 1650 (4~GB, sm\_75, no tensor cores),
i5-11400H, 16~GB RAM. Mixed precision throughout; transformer runs use batch 8
with 4-step accumulation for an effective batch of 32. Peak memory is dominated
by optimiser state, not activations --- fusion costs about 14~MB more than the
text encoder alone.

\textbf{Protocol, fixed before any result was read.} Per-tag thresholds are
tuned on validation, frozen, then applied to test, which is touched exactly once
per run. Node-feature and mel normalisation statistics come from the training
split only, and the pipeline refuses to run against a statistics file that does
not record that provenance. Artist-disjointness is asserted at every run start.

\textbf{Fairness: compute budget, not parameter count.}
\label{sec:fairness}
An earlier version sized the CNN baseline's channels to match the GNN's
parameter count, reasoning that equal capacity was fair. That was wrong and it
produced a misleading result (Section~\ref{sec:b2}): convolutional weights are
reused at every time--frequency position, so equal parameters buy the two
architectures very unequal computation, and matching them starves the CNN. We
equalise the compute budget instead --- same GPU, epoch cap and early-stopping
rule --- and report both parameter counts and wall-clock so the reader sees what
each model cost.

\subsection{Task 2: genre classification on FMA-small}
Table~\ref{tab:genre} reports the headline Task 2 result: eight-way
single-label classification over FMA-small. The split is near-balanced
(797--801 training clips per class, 100--101 test clips), so chance sits at
12.5\% and plain accuracy is meaningful here. It is the only table in this work
that reports accuracy; for multi-label tagging it never appears, for reasons
Section~\ref{sec:tagging} makes concrete.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Task 2 headline: FMA-small eight-way genre, test split
(\FMATestRows{} clips). Chance accuracy is 12.5\%. The GNN is reported over
\TTwoGenreSeeds{} seeds; B2 is a single seed, so its numbers carry no spread
and the comparison is read accordingly. Neither row is bolded: see the text.}
\label{tab:genre}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Model & Acc. & Macro-F1 & Params & Wall-clock \\
\midrule
B2 mel CNN (1 seed) & \BTwoGenreAcc{} & \BTwoGenreF{} & \BTwoGenreParams{} & \BTwoGenreTime{} \\
T2 GNN (\TTwoGenreSeeds{} seeds) & \TTwoGenreAccMean{} & \TTwoGenreFMean{} & \TTwoGenreParams{} & \TTwoGenreTime{} \\
\quad seed spread & $\pm$\TTwoGenreAccSd{} & $\pm$\TTwoGenreFSd{} & & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\label{sec:b2fair}
\textbf{The CNN baseline outscores the GNN, and we report it that way.} B2
reaches \BTwoGenreAcc{} accuracy and \BTwoGenreF{} macro-F1 against the GNN's
\TTwoGenreAccMean{} and \TTwoGenreFMean{}. We fixed before running B2 that if it
won it would be reported as the headline and the GNN would not be re-tuned to
chase it, and that is what happens here --- no GNN hyperparameter was changed
after seeing this table.

Two things temper it in both directions. The GNN's seed spread is
$\pm$\TTwoGenreAccSd{} points and B2 is a single seed, so the gap is not
cleanly separable and no ordering is claimed. But B2 needs roughly ten times the
parameters and ten times the wall-clock to reach it, and it reads
full-resolution spectrograms where the GNN reads pooled segment statistics at
roughly one per second. The comparison measures representation granularity, not
the value of graph structure; the controls that isolate structure are B4 and the
rewiring ablation, both on the GNN's own features, and the Task 2 structural
claim rests on those rather than on this row.

\textbf{Where the errors go is more informative than the diagonal.}
Fig.~\ref{fig:confusion} (Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative}) shows the confusion
structure is far from uniform.
Hip-Hop is the most separable class and Electronic the next, which is what one
would expect from a representation built on rhythmic and spectral segment
statistics. The failures cluster: Folk is predicted as Experimental more often
than as Folk, and Instrumental scatters into Folk and Experimental rather than
being confused broadly. That pattern is a property of the label set as much as
of the model -- ``Instrumental'' and ``Experimental'' are not acoustically
disjoint categories, and a recording can satisfy both descriptions without any
annotation error. Reporting only the aggregate accuracy would hide this
entirely, which is why the matrix is reported alongside it.

\label{sec:tagging}

it is the only corpus here whose label space Task 3 also uses, which is what
makes Tasks 2 and 3 comparable at all.

\textbf{What the audio-only rows say.} B4 mean-pools the \emph{same}
96-dimensional segment features and feeds them to an MLP, so it is the ``do you
even need a graph?'' control. The gap between the GNN and B4 --- not the gap to
random --- is the graph structure's actual contribution, and it is
\BFourDelta{} macro-F1: about \BFourDeltaFloors{}$\times$ the measurement floor
(Section~\ref{sec:noisefloor}). That is a real effect and a modest one. We state
the multiple because ``separable'' and ``large'' are different claims, and only
the first is supported here.

\textbf{Task 3 scores below Task 2 on tags, and the reason is not the fusion.}
The T3 row is a multi-task model splitting its capacity and its batches between
50-way tagging and DEAM valence/arousal regression at a 4:1 batch ratio, and it
converged in \TThreeHeadEpochs{} epochs of a \TThreeHeadTime{} budget where the
tags-only GNN had \TTwoTagParams{} parameters to spend on one objective. Its
tag macro-F1 is therefore the price of the emotion head, not evidence that
fusion hurts. What it buys is in Section~\ref{sec:emotion}, which the Task 2
model cannot produce at all.

\textbf{Text alone is weak on MagnaTagATune, as expected.} The BERT row reaches
only \TOneMtatF{} macro-F1 from \texttt{clip\_info} metadata, and its validation
score peaked early before declining. MagnaTagATune ships no captions, and an
artist name is close to uninformative about which of 50 tags applies. This is
the low end of the text-informativeness axis whose high end
Section~\ref{sec:leakage} anchors.

\subsection{B2: what fixing the baseline changed}
\label{sec:b2}
The parameter-matched CNN scored 0.1654 macro-F1, below the PCA+MLP control on
the same audio -- not a credible architecture result. Three causes were
identified and all three were the experimental design's fault rather than the
CNN's. Parameter matching starved it (Section~\ref{sec:fairness}). The mel cache
was mean-pooled to 256 columns per track, about 8.8 frames per second, so a
3-second window was 26 columns wide -- far too coarse for a convolutional stack
whose premise is local time--frequency structure. And it consumed one global
descriptor per 29-second clip, asking a single vector to explain 50 local tags.

The rebuilt baseline is the standard short-chunk CNN \cite{won2020eval}: seven
$3{\times}3$ convolution blocks with $2{\times}2$ pooling, \BTwoTagParams{}
parameters, trained on random 3-second excerpts of a native-resolution mel cache
at 43.07 frames per second, with per-chunk probabilities averaged over nine
evenly spaced excerpts at inference. The cache is 4.0~GB for MagnaTagATune and
1.6~GB for FMA-small at float16 with gzip; that storage cost is why the pooled
cache existed, and paying it is what the fix required.

\subsection{Task 1 and the cost of not masking}
\label{sec:leakage}
MusicCaps captions are written \emph{from} the aspect list that also supplies
the labels, so a raw caption contains its own labels almost verbatim.
Table~\ref{tab:musiccaps} reports runs identical except for whether those label
terms are masked out of the input.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Task 1 on MusicCaps, test split (\MCTest{} clips, 50 MusicCaps
aspects). \emph{Not comparable with Table~\ref{tab:mtat}}: different corpus,
different label vocabulary, different split.}
\label{tab:musiccaps}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Text input & Freeze & Macro-F1 & @0.5 & Micro-F1 & AUC-PR \\
\midrule
\texttt{caption\_masked} & probe   & \MCProbeF{} & --- & \MCProbeMicro{} & \MCProbePR{} \\
\texttt{caption\_masked} & top-$n$ & \MCTopNF{} & --- & \MCTopNMicro{} & \MCTopNPR{} \\
\texttt{caption\_masked} & full FT & \textbf{\MCMaskedF{}} & \MCMaskedFixed{} & \MCMaskedMicro{} & \MCMaskedPR{} \\
\texttt{caption\_raw}    & full FT & \MCRawF{} & \MCRawFixed{} & \MCRawMicro{} & \MCRawPR{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{The leakage gap is \LeakGap{} macro-F1, a \LeakPct{}\% relative
inflation.} The two runs are the same model at the same capacity
(\MCRawParams{} trainable parameters), same split, same schedule, same threshold
protocol; the only difference is whether label terms were removed from the input
text, so the gap is attributable to leakage and nothing else. The headline Task
1 number is the masked \MCMaskedF{}. Reporting \MCRawF{} without this caveat
would overstate the result by more than half --- and that is the easy mistake,
because unmasked is what a reader gets by default.

\textbf{The freeze modes separate cleanly, and monotonically with trainable
capacity.} A frozen encoder with only a \MCProbeParams{}-parameter head reaches
\MCProbeF{}; unfreezing the top four layers (\MCTopNParams{} parameters) reaches
\MCTopNF{}; full fine-tuning (\MCMaskedParams{}) reaches \MCMaskedF{}. The gaps
are far larger than the threshold-resampling spread of
Section~\ref{sec:thresholds}, so this ordering is a result rather than noise.

That it is reportable at all took a fix. In the first sweep
\texttt{bert.freeze\_mode} was not honoured, so the run labelled \emph{frozen
probe} trained every parameter and duplicated full fine-tuning: two of the three
modes were the same experiment and the ``ordering'' between them was CUDA
non-determinism. The rows above are a re-run against the train-only vocabulary,
distinct by construction --- their trainable parameter counts differ by three
orders of magnitude.

\textbf{Fine-tuning still overfits.} Validation macro-F1 reaches \MCMaskedVal{}
against \MCMaskedF{} on test: with \MCTrain{} training rows against 109M
parameters the model fits the \MCVal{}-row validation split long before it
generalises, and the test split is the AudioSet evaluation partition rather than
a random holdout. The fine-tuning gain is real, but read it from the test column
only.

\subsection{DEAM emotion regression}
\label{sec:emotion}
The multi-task loss carries valence and arousal regression as $\mathcal{L}_
{\text{aux}}$. Targets are standardised with training-split statistics before
the MSE; predictions are inverted before scoring, so MAE and RMSE below are on
DEAM's original \EmoScale{} scale, while $R^2$ is affine-invariant and reads the
same either way.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{DEAM valence and arousal, test split (\EmoN{} tracks), from the
full-budget multi-task Task 3 run. MAE and RMSE are on the 1--9 scale. The
right-hand column is the $R^2$ spread over seeds 42/1337/2024 at the fixed
ablation budget.}
\label{tab:emotion}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Target & MAE & RMSE & $R^2$ & $R^2$ over 3 seeds \\
\midrule
Valence & \EmoValMAE{} & \EmoValRMSE{} & \EmoValRTwo{} & \EmoValRTwoMean{} $\pm$ \EmoValRTwoSd{} \\
Arousal & \EmoAroMAE{} & \EmoAroRMSE{} & \EmoAroRTwo{} & \EmoAroRTwoMean{} $\pm$ \EmoAroRTwoSd{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{Arousal is learnable from this representation; valence is much less so.}
Arousal reaches $R^2 = \EmoAroRTwo{}$ and valence \EmoValRTwo{}, and the seed
spread separates them further: arousal is stable at
\EmoAroRTwoMean{} $\pm$ \EmoAroRTwoSd{} while valence swings
\EmoValRTwoMean{} $\pm$ \EmoValRTwoSd{} --- a standard deviation more than half
its own mean. We report the spread rather than the best seed because a single
valence number from this setup is not reproducible.

The asymmetry is the expected one and it is informative. Arousal tracks energy,
density and tempo, which segment-level spectral and rhythmic statistics
represent directly. Valence tracks something closer to mode, harmony and lyrical
affect, of which the node features encode very little and the MagnaTagATune text
channel --- title, album, artist --- encodes none. The emotion head is an
auxiliary term on \EmoN{} test tracks, not a competitive DEAM model, and these
numbers should be read as evidence that the multi-task plumbing works and that
the representation carries arousal better than valence.

\subsection{What the fused representation separates}
\label{sec:tsne}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tsne_panels.png}
\caption{t-SNE of the fused representation $\mathbf{z}$, perplexity
\TsnePerplexity{} in all three panels. (a) FMA genre, \TsneGenreN{} clips,
k-NN probe \TsneGenreKnn{}, silhouette \TsneGenreSil{}. (b) DEAM
valence/arousal quadrants, \TsneMoodN{} clips, probe \TsneMoodKnn{},
silhouette \TsneMoodSil{}. (c) MagnaTagATune mood tags, \TsneMtatN{} clips,
probe \TsneMtatKnn{}, silhouette \TsneMtatSil{}; \TsneMtatExcluded{} clips
match no mood tag and are excluded rather than pooled into an ``other'' class
that would be trivially separable. The probe numbers are the evidence; the
picture is illustration.}
\label{fig:tsne}
\end{figure}

Fig.~\ref{fig:tsne} makes a point the accuracy tables cannot. All three
silhouettes are near zero or negative --- \TsneGenreSil{}, \TsneMoodSil{} and
\TsneMtatSil{} --- so the classes do \emph{not} form separated clusters in the
embedding. Yet the k-NN probes reach \TsneGenreKnn{} and \TsneMoodKnn{} against
chance of 0.125 and 0.25. The information is there and it is locally
recoverable; it is simply not arranged as globally separated blobs, which is
the usual state of affairs and the reason we report the probe rather than
inviting the reader to judge the picture.

Panel (c) is labelled for what it is. Per Section~\ref{sec:fairness}, 7 of the
15 affect words we wanted are absent from MagnaTagATune's top-50, so what
remains --- soft, hard, ambient, quiet, loud, slow, fast, weird --- describes
texture and dynamics rather than emotion. The affect story is panel (b), on
DEAM's annotated valence and arousal.

\textbf{The $S_{\text{graph}}$ control is saturated and we report it as such}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:diagnostics}, Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostics}).
Real graphs score \SGraphReal{} against \SGraphRewired{} for degree-preserving
rewired ones --- a difference of about 0.011. The reason is visible in the
inputs: mean edge cosine is \SGraphEdgeCos{} against a threshold of
$\tau = \SGraphTau{}$, so nearly every edge clears the bar whether or not the
topology means anything, and the statistic has almost no room to discriminate.
This is a defect in the metric's threshold, not evidence that rewiring is
harmless; the rewiring result that \emph{does} discriminate is the downstream
macro-F1 comparison in Section~\ref{sec:fusion}. We report the number because
it was pre-registered as an analysis, and we decline to draw a conclusion from
it.

\label{sec:contrast}
That null is only interpretable next to its opposite. Table~\ref{tab:contrast}
runs three of the same modes on MusicCaps, where the text is a written
description of the music rather than an artist name.

\caption{The same fusion modes on two corpora, seed 42. MagnaTagATune's text is
\texttt{clip\_info} metadata; MusicCaps' is a masked caption. The corpora have
different label vocabularies, so compare \emph{within} a column, never across.}
\label{tab:contrast}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Mode & MTAT (metadata) & MusicCaps (caption) \\
\midrule
\texttt{bert\_only}      & \AblationBertOnly{} & \MCBertOnly{} \\

\textbf{Which modality dominates flips with the corpus, and the flip is large.}
On MagnaTagATune the graph carries the task and text contributes nothing; on
MusicCaps the ordering inverts --- text alone reaches \MCBertOnly{} while the
graph alone manages only \MCGnnOnly{}, and fusion is the best of the three at
\MCCrossAttention{}. The architecture is identical in both columns. What changed
is how much the text knows.

This is the contrast the two-corpus design was built to produce, and it is a
more useful claim than either column alone: fusion is not intrinsically
worthwhile, it is worthwhile in proportion to what the second modality
contributes. A single-corpus study would have reported whichever half it
happened to run and drawn the opposite conclusion.

The same budget caveat applies across corpora: MusicCaps
\texttt{cross\_attention} reaches \MCCrossAttention{} here against Task 1's
standalone \MCMaskedF{} in Table~\ref{tab:musiccaps}, and that gap is the
reduced ablation budget rather than evidence that fusion costs accuracy.

We resist reading the MusicCaps margin of fusion over \texttt{bert\_only}
(\MCCrossAttention{} against \MCBertOnly{}) as meaningful. It is small, it is
one seed, and the floor in Section~\ref{sec:noisefloor} was measured on
MagnaTagATune's validation split rather than this one. The claim we make is the
reordering, which is an order of magnitude larger than any of these gaps.

\subsection{Task 4: contrastive graph--caption retrieval}
\label{sec:retrieval}
Retrieval is reported over \FourSeeds{} seeds and both directions against a
gallery of \FourGallery{} MusicCaps test clips. At that gallery size a recall
is uninterpretable without its chance value, so both are given.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Task 4 retrieval, mean over \FourSeeds{} seeds and both directions,
gallery \FourGallery{}. Chance is analytic ($K/N$), not estimated.}
\label{tab:retrieval}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Metric & Model & Chance & Lift \\
\midrule
R@1     & \FourRAtOne{}  & \FourChanceOne{}  & \FourLiftOne{}$\times$ \\
R@5     & \FourRAtFive{} & \FourChanceFive{} & \FourLiftFive{}$\times$ \\
R@10    & \FourRAtTen{}  & \FourChanceTen{}  & \FourLiftTen{}$\times$ \\
MRR     & \FourMRR{}     & \FourChanceMRR{}  & --- \\
median rank & \FourMedR{} & \FourChanceMedR{} & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{The model learns something, and not much.} R@10 is
$\FourRAtTen{} \pm \FourRAtTenSd{}$ against a chance value of
\FourChanceTen{} --- a lift of \FourLiftTen{}$\times$, consistent across all
three recall depths and stable across seeds. The median true clip sits at rank
\FourMedR{} of \FourGallery{} where chance would put it at \FourChanceMedR{}.
The two directions agree (graph-to-text \FourGtoT{}, text-to-graph
\FourTtoG{}), so nothing here rests on which modality is the query.

\textbf{The first version of this run was undertrained, not data-limited, and
it is worth saying which.} At a contrastive batch of 512 over \MCTrain{}
training pairs, an epoch is four optimiser steps, so early stopping fired after
a few hundred updates and the run finished in minutes. Re-running at batch
\FourBatch{} --- quadrupling the steps per epoch at a comparable in-batch
negative count, with the architecture untouched --- lifted R@10 from
\FourPrevRAtTen{} to \FourRAtTen{}, and the lift over chance from
\FourPrevLift{}$\times$ to \FourLiftTen{}$\times$. Validation R@10 peaked at
epoch \FourBestEpoch{} of \FourEpochs{} run, so the model then converged rather
than being cut short again. We report the earlier number alongside because the
difference between ``the data is too small'' and ``we did not train it long
enough'' is exactly the kind of claim that should be tested before it is made.

Having tested it, the data limit is now the earned reading rather than the
assumed one. An R@10 of \FourRAtTen{} looks like failure and a lift of
\FourLiftTen{}$\times$ looks like success; they are the same number. With
\MCTrain{} pairs against the tens of millions used by MuLan
\cite{huang2022mulan} and CLAP \cite{elizalde2023clap}, what the model recovers
is a weak but real and reproducible signal, not a usable retrieval system.
Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative} shows where it fails and by how far.

\subsection{Threshold stability}
\label{sec:thresholds}
Every multi-label number above is reported at per-tag thresholds fitted on
validation. That fit is a fit like any other, and MagnaTagATune's validation
split is 977 clips from 14 artists -- small, and correlated within artist. We
resample the validation rows with replacement \NBoot{} times, re-tune all 50
thresholds on each replicate, and apply each threshold vector unchanged to the
fixed test split. Table~\ref{tab:boot} reports the resulting spread.

%% bootstrap table moved to the appendix (D5 step 1)


\textbf{What moves, and what does not.} Across replicates the tuned test
macro-F1 has a standard deviation of \BootLeadStd{} and a 95\% interval of
\BootLeadCI{}; the full range over all \NBoot{} replicates is
\BootLeadSpread{}. These are three different statistics and it matters which one
a claim rests on: by the interval the headline number is
$\BootLeadTuned{} \pm 0.011$, which is tight, but the range is what a single
unlucky validation draw could actually produce, and it exceeds the 0.02 limit.
\BootVerdict

Tuning is not cosmetic -- it is worth \BootLeadTuned{} against \BootLeadFixed{}
at a fixed 0.5 threshold, roughly $+0.08$ macro-F1 -- so the answer is to report
both rather than to abandon tuning.

\textbf{The instability is concentrated in the rare tags.} Mean per-tag
threshold standard deviation is \BootThrStdMean{} against a maximum of
\BootThrStdMax{}; the five least stable (\BootWorstTags{}) are all
low-frequency. With \BootValRows{} validation clips, a tag appearing in a few
dozen has almost no positives left after resampling, so its threshold is barely
identified and the tuner fits noise. That is a property of the split size, not
the tuning procedure, and it is why macro-F1 --- weighting rare tags equally ---
carries more variance here than micro-F1.

% ===========================================================================
\subsection{The measurement floor, and what it forbids}
\label{sec:noisefloor}
The bootstrap in Section~\ref{sec:thresholds} is usually read as a caveat on one
table. It is better understood as a property of the experimental setup as a
whole: on MagnaTagATune, resampling the validation split moves the tuned test
macro-F1 over a range of \BootLeadSpread{}. Nothing measured through that
validation split can resolve a difference smaller than this, whatever it is a
difference between.

We apply that as a rule rather than a disclaimer. Every ablation row carries
mean and standard deviation over three seeds, since the ablation table is
exactly where a lucky seed gets promoted to a finding; every table carries the
untuned fixed-0.5 column beside the tuned one; every ablation caption states the
\BootLeadSpread{} figure and reports a $\Delta$-vs-best column, so a reader can
see which rows are separable; and where rows fall inside the floor we say they
are within noise of each other and decline to rank them.

The fourth point is the one that costs something, so it is worth being explicit
about why we pay it. A ranked list of seven fusion modes reported to four
decimal places looks like a more substantial result than ``these four are
indistinguishable and these three are worse''. It is not. The first invites the
reader to believe a precision the measurement does not support, and any
follow-up work that tried to build on the ordering would be building on noise.
Reporting a measured floor and then respecting it is the stronger claim, and it
is a claim about the experiment rather than about the model.

We note that this floor is a property of \emph{this} validation split --- 977
clips from 14 artists --- and not an intrinsic limit of the task. A larger
validation set would lower it. Reporting the number makes that trade visible;
reporting only point estimates would not.

\textbf{Qualitative material is in Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative}.} Ten
retrieval queries plotted by the rank their true clip received, and three Task 3
case studies with graph attention and caption alignment, are reported there
rather than here: they illustrate the numbers above without adding evidence to
them, and the page budget is better spent on the results themselves.

\section{Human Evaluation}
\label{sec:human}
% ===========================================================================
\HERaters{} listeners rated \HEItems{} caption--clip pairs on a 1--5 match scale
in randomised order, \HEControls{} of them deliberately mismatched controls,
giving \HERatings{} ratings --- above the five-rater minimum the brief sets.

\textbf{Control discrimination, first.} Genuine pairs averaged \HEMeanReal{} and
control pairs \HEMeanControl{}: a gap of \HEGap{}, in the wrong direction, at
$p = \HEGapP{}$ (one-sided Mann--Whitney). Raters did not separate true pairings
from mismatched ones. This is reported before the ratings because it governs how
they may be read: \HEVerdict{}. The mean rating below is \emph{not} evidence
that retrieved captions describe their clips, and is not used as such anywhere
in this work.

\textbf{The ratings, under that constraint.} Mean match was
$\HEMean{} \pm \HESd{}$. Inter-rater agreement was $\alpha = \HEAlpha{}$
(Krippendorff, ordinal) with mean pairwise Spearman
$\HESpearman{} \pm \HESpearmanSd{}$ over \HEPairs{} rater pairs --- above
chance, but far below the $0.667$ conventionally treated as a floor for drawing
even tentative conclusions from an annotation.

\textbf{The panel was attending; the controls failed.} A null control gap has
two explanations with very different costs. Ratings differ sharply across items:
Kruskal--Wallis $H = \HEBetweenH{}$, $p = \HEBetweenP{}$, with
\HEVarShare{}\% of rating variance falling between items rather than within
them, and real-item means spanning \HEItemMin{} to \HEItemMax{} --- nearly the
full scale. Listeners clicking at random produce neither. The panel
discriminated between clips; what it failed to discriminate was the
manipulation.

The construction is why. \HEReused{} of the \HEControls{} controls carry a
caption that also appears on a real item in the same sheet, paired there with
its true clip; a rater meeting one description twice over different audio cannot
tell which pairing is wrong. Those captions also survive reshuffling: one reused
``a male singer\ldots{} hip hop\ldots{} slick drumming rhythm, groovy bass
line'', which any hip-hop clip satisfies, and scored \emph{above} its genuine
counterpart (4.70 against 4.10). The one control with a unique caption described
recording conditions --- ``poorly recorded live sound check\ldots{} low fidelity
with ambient noise'' --- and scored 4.20, because low-fidelity clips are common
in MusicCaps and that description transfers freely.

This converges with the case studies (Fig.~\ref{fig:cases}): the captions the
model gets right also describe \emph{recording conditions} rather than musical
content. Two judges, one learned and one human, are limited by the same corpus
property --- these descriptions carry little clip-specific information.

\textbf{What this costs.} The listening study contributes no validation of
retrieval quality; Task 4's R@10 of \FourRAtTen{} at
\FourLiftTen{}$\times$ chance (Section~\ref{sec:retrieval}) stands on its
automatic evaluation alone and is not corroborated here. Repairing the study
needs controls drawn from acoustically distant clips with captions appearing
exactly once --- a redesign, not a reanalysis, and out of scope for this
submission. It is reported in full because a study that fails its own validity
check misleads only when the failure is omitted.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Limitations}
Stated in rough order of how much they constrain the conclusions.

\textbf{The measurement floor.} Differences below \BootLeadSpread{} macro-F1 on
MagnaTagATune are not resolvable through this validation split
(Section~\ref{sec:noisefloor}). Several comparisons we would like to make ---
particularly among fusion modes --- fall inside it.

\textbf{B2 and the GNN do not see the same input} --- full-resolution
spectrograms at 43.07 frames per second against 96-dimen\-sional pooled segment
statistics at roughly one per second. No comparison between them isolates graph
structure, which is why the structural claim rests on B4 and the rewiring
ablation instead (Section~\ref{sec:b2fair}).

\textbf{MusicCaps attrition is not random.} Survival correlates with video age,
region and channel deletion (Section~\ref{sec:methodology}), so the
\MCTest{}-clip evaluation set is a biased sample. Reporting the gallery size
with every R@$K$ is necessary but not sufficient: the sample is
non-representative in a direction we cannot measure.

\textbf{The chord figure is not an audio result.} The 77.4\% is measured on
MIDI-derived chroma, not audio. Real recordings add polyphony, percussion,
reverb and mastering, all of which smear chroma, so that number should not be
read as an audio-domain chord accuracy; none is claimed here.

\textbf{The validation split is thin.} 977 clips from 14 artists is small and
correlated within artist, which produces the floor above and leaves the rare
tags --- weighted equally by macro-F1 --- with very few positives to fit a
threshold on.

\textbf{Mood labels are constructed, not annotated.} Neither corpus ships a mood
field. The DEAM quadrants are a midpoint split of continuous annotations --- a
defensible convention, still a discretisation we chose. The MagnaTagATune mood
set is worse: 7 of the 15 affect words we wanted are absent from its top-50, and
what remains describes texture and dynamics rather than emotion.

\textbf{Task 4 is trained on \MCTrain{} pairs.} Contrastive alignment is a
data-hungry recipe: MuLan \cite{huang2022mulan} consumes roughly 44 million
audio--text pairs, four orders of magnitude more. The \FourLiftTen{}$\times$
lift over chance should be read as evidence that the recipe transfers to a
segment-graph encoder at small scale, not as a usable retrieval system.

\textbf{The listening study's controls were not controls.} \HEReused{} of
\HEControls{} reused a caption that a real item in the same sheet also carried,
and the captions were generic enough that a randomly paired clip still
satisfied them, so the study cannot validate retrieval quality
(Section~\ref{sec:human}). The panel was demonstrably attending; the defect is
in our construction, and repairing it needs controls drawn from acoustically
distant clips with captions used exactly once.

\textbf{Single-corpus emotion supervision.} Valence and arousal come from DEAM
alone, so the regression results should not be read as corpus-independent.

\textbf{Scale.} A single 4~GB GPU caps batch size and model size. Memory is
dominated by optimiser state rather than activations, so the binding constraint
is wall-clock rather than capacity, but it is still a constraint: the seed
sweeps and the seven-mode ablation are what it limits.

\section{Conclusion}
% ===========================================================================
A shared segment-graph representation supports tagging, genre classification,
fusion and retrieval without task-specific preprocessing, and the graph's
contribution is measurable against a mean-pooling control on identical features.
The more transferable findings are methodological. Caption corpora derived from
their own label sets inflate results by more than half unless the labels are
masked out of the input; standard splits are not always disjoint in the way
their documentation implies; and selecting a label vocabulary by corpus-wide
frequency leaks test information before training begins. Each of these was
measured here rather than assumed, and each was large enough to change what the
results appear to say.

The listening study makes the same point against us. Its controls failed their
own validity check (Section~\ref{sec:human}), so it validates nothing --- and we
only know that because the check was built into the design rather than added
once the mean looked reasonable. A study without that check would have reported
a mean of \HEMean{} and called it corroboration.

\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}
Every number in this paper is generated from files in the repository by
\texttt{report/fill\_report.py}, which rewrites a block of macro definitions
from \texttt{results/*.json}. The prose contains no literal figures, so a stale
number cannot survive a re-run; a result that has not been produced yet renders
as \emph{pending} and the script names it.

\textbf{Hardware.} One NVIDIA GTX 1650 (4~GB, compute capability 7.5, no tensor
cores), Intel i5-11400H, 16~GB RAM. Mixed precision throughout. The transformer
sweeps were also run on a Kaggle T4; results agreed to four decimal places where
both were run.

\textbf{Seeds.} 42, 1337 and 2024 for every reported ablation row and headline
result. The B1/B2/B4 baselines are single-seed (42) and are labelled as such
wherever they appear beside a multi-seed row. Seeding covers Python, NumPy, torch and the dataloader workers;
determinism is not otherwise forced, so single-run numbers carry CUDA
non-determinism on the order of $10^{-3}$ --- an order of magnitude below the
measurement floor, and one reason the floor rather than the seed spread is the
binding constraint.

\textbf{Splits and statistics.} Splits are artist-disjoint within and across
corpora, asserted at the start of every training job. Feature normalisation, mel
normalisation, emotion target scaling and the tag vocabularies are all computed
on the training split only; each artifact records that provenance and the
pipeline refuses to run against one that does not.

\textbf{Thresholds.} Tuned on validation, frozen, then applied once to test. The
test split is read exactly once per run, after both the model and the thresholds
are final.

\textbf{Listening study.} The presentation order, the control assignments and
the item-to-clip mapping are fixed by \texttt{sheet\_key.json}, written by
\texttt{scripts/make\_listening\_page.py} under a recorded seed. The
de-identified ratings (\texttt{raw\_responses.csv}, timestamps only --- no
identifying fields were collected) and the reshaped long form are committed;
\texttt{scripts/analyse\_human\_eval.py} regenerates every number in
Section~\ref{sec:human} from them, and refuses to guess when the form columns
do not line up with the key.

\textbf{Commands.} The full pipeline is
\begin{verbatim}
make verify-data      # check every file exists and decodes
make splits           # manifests + artist-disjoint repair
make vocab            # train-only tag vocabularies
make features graphs  # 96-dim cache, segment graphs
make mel-cache        # full-resolution mels for B2
make all-tasks        # tasks 1-4, all seeds
make baselines        # B1, B2, B4
make thresholds       # bootstrap the operating point
make evaluate         # tables and figures
make human-eval       # listening sheet, then ratings analysis
make report           # fill and check the LaTeX
\end{verbatim}

\section{Per-Tag Threshold Stability}
\label{app:thresholds}
Section~\ref{sec:thresholds} reports the aggregate effect of resampling the
validation split. This appendix carries the per-tag detail, which is the part
that explains \emph{why} the aggregate moves: the instability is not spread
evenly across the vocabulary but concentrated in the rare tags, whose thresholds
are fitted on a handful of positive examples.
